subtype: Approach: demanding and arguing [Pitfall]
passage: The concert started at seven, it was already five, and Baljeet still didn't have permission. He found his parents in the kitchen, both tired after a long day at the shop. "I'm going to the concert tonight with Harjot and them." "Where is it? Who's driving? When does it end?" Mummy asked. "Why does it matter? Everyone else is allowed! You're the strictest parents in the whole school!" Papa put down his cup. "Don't shout in this house." "I'm not shouting!" he shouted. His sister Ritu, doing homework at the table, slowly slid her books out of the room. Each question from Mummy got a louder answer. By a quarter to six Papa said, very quietly, "No. Not tonight. And we'll talk about next month's trip too." Baljeet slammed his door. Harjot's texts kept coming: "where r u??"

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and panicky with time running out, and it came out as angry shouting.

qa.a: Ritu seemed uncomfortable, quietly sliding her books out of the room to escape the shouting.

subtype: Approach: building trust through track record [Action]

Papa lowered the newspaper. "Try me."
"For the last six weeks I've been home by eight every time. Every single time. I message when I reach Divyansh's and when I leave."
"I've noticed."
"And I've done the dustbin and the milk every morning without being reminded."
Mummy called from the kitchen, "That's true, actually."
"So," Mridul said, "can eight become nine on Saturdays? Same messages. Same everything."
Papa folded the paper slowly. "You planned this speech."
"I planned the six weeks. The speech is short."
Papa laughed despite himself. "Nine on Saturdays. Keep the messages."
"Deal."

subtype: Approach: building trust through track record [Action]
passage: I'm Simran, and last year I learnt that arguing with my parents about curfew gets me nowhere, but a notebook does. When they said no to the evening coding club, which ends at 8:30, I didn't argue. I just started keeping a record. Every time I went out, I wrote down the time I said I'd be back and the time I actually was. I messaged Mumma when I reached places and when I left. I did the dishes every night without being asked, which my brother Kishore found deeply suspicious. After two months the notebook had forty-one entries, every one on time, one of them early. I showed it to Mumma and Papa on a Sunday. Papa turned the pages slowly. "Coding club," he said. "Tuesdays. Kishore picks you up."

qa.a: Kishore, who found the dishwashing suspicious, now has pick-up duty, which he may grumble about but which shows he is trusted too.

Instead, both of them took an auto to the new mall in Noida, bought bubble tea and wandered round till seven. Vasudha's mother said the girls hadn't been there all afternoon. When Parul walked in, her mother didn't shout. She just held out her hand for the phone. subtype: Approach: choosing timing and mood for the talk [Thinking]
passage: I'm Suraj, and I learnt about timing by getting it wrong. The first time I asked Papa about the overnight trek with Sahil's family, it was a Thursday night. Papa had just come off a twelve-hour shift and was eating dinner standing up. He said no before I finished the sentence. The second time was worse: the day my Maths result came back with a 52. He's always easiest on Sunday afternoons, after lunch, with the cricket on and nowhere to be. So I waited a whole week. That Sunday I sat next to him during a slow over and asked properly, with all the details. He listened to every word. He said he'd call Sahil's father.

qa.a: Bring all the details, who is going, where they will stay and when they will be back, so Papa can say yes without worrying.

subtype: Approach: choosing timing and mood for the talk [Thinking]
passage:
Counsellor's note, 10 October — Pranav, Class 11
Pranav came in frustrated last week: every time he asked his father about joining the weekend football league, the answer was no. We went through when he had asked. Monday, right after his father got home from the night shift. Then the evening the half-yearly Physics mark came in. Then during a family argument about bills. I asked what his father is like on a relaxed day. Pranav thought, then said, "Sunday morning, after his walk, when he reads the paper." He decided to try then, with the league timings written down. Today he told me it went differently. His father asked questions instead of saying no, and agreed to a trial month. Pranav said, "Same question. Different day."
— Uday

subtype: Approach: involving a trusted relative as mediator [Action]

Dear Rekha Maasi,
Thank you for Sunday. I know it wasn't fun sitting between me and Mummy while we both tried to talk at once. You were right that I only ever asked to go to the college fest, never how I'd get there and back. And Mummy listened to you in a way she hasn't listened to me for weeks. When you asked her what exactly worried her, and she said "the road home at ten", I finally understood. The middle path we found is fair: I go to the fest but leave at eight, and Sahil Bhaiya drops and collects me on his scooter. Mummy even smiled at the end. I'll send you a photo from the fest. I owe you a big plate of your favourite jalebis.
Love,
Uma

subtype: Approach: involving a trusted relative as mediator [Action]

passage: Sofia's curfew in Seville was ten, and she walked through the door at 10:50. Her father, Javier, was sitting in the hall in his coat, phone in hand. Before he could speak, she said, "I'm sorry. I'm late, and I didn't call. That's on me." He waited. "We missed the last tram because I wanted to stay for one more song. Then my phone died. That's the reason, but it's not an excuse." Javier took off his coat slowly. "I was about to go looking for you." "I know. So here's what I want to do: for the next two weekends I'll text you every hour, and I'll be home by half past nine, not ten. I'll carry a power bank. Then we can see." Her father looked at her for a long moment. "Every hour," he said. "And the power bank."

subtype: Approach: reviewing after a broken agreement [Revision]

subtype: Approach: accepting a partial win [Revision]
passage:
Counsellor's note, 5 December — Tanvir, Class 12
Tanvir had asked his parents to let him stay out till eleven on Saturdays. They agreed to nine. He came in today expecting me to help him "fight for the other two hours". We talked it through instead. I asked what nine gets him. He thought about it: the film, dinner with friends, the auto ride home before the roads empty. "Most of it," he admitted. We wrote a review date on his calendar, 15 January. If he keeps to nine every Saturday until then, he will ask for ten. He said, "If I fight for eleven now, I'll probably get nothing. If I keep nine for six weeks, ten is easy." He looked annoyed for about a minute, and then quite pleased with himself.
— Hafsa

qa.q: What is Tanvir's review date?
qa.a: 15 January.

qa.q: How did Tanvir seem to feel by the end?
qa.a: He looked annoyed for about a minute, then quite pleased with himself for the plan.

qa.q: Why might accepting nine lead to more freedom than fighting for eleven?
qa.a: Keeping nine steadily builds a record that makes ten an easy next step, while fighting now might lose everything.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's parents see him accepting nine?
qa.a: They may be relieved and more trusting, seeing him accept their limit calmly and plan for a fair review.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen accepting an earlier hour than asked, setting a review date and aiming for gradual gains.

subtype: Approach: understanding the situation openly [Thinking]
passage: For two weeks the flat in Buenos Aires had felt different. Papá was home at odd hours, Mamá kept doing sums on the backs of envelopes, and conversations stopped when Sofia walked in. Her little brother Diego asked if their parents were getting divorced. Sofia didn't think so, but she couldn't sleep either. On Sunday, while Mamá washed up, Sofia dried the plates beside her and said quietly, "Something's changed. Can you tell me what?" Mamá's hands stopped. Then she told her: the shop where Papá worked had cut his hours in half. Nobody was ill, nobody was leaving. There was just less money for a while, so no big purchases, and the holiday was off. Sofia felt something unknot in her chest. It was a hard problem. But it was a real one, with edges.

qa.q: What had happened to Papá's work?
qa.a: The shop where he worked had cut his hours in half.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel once Mamá explained?
qa.a: She felt relieved, something unknotting in her chest, because a clear problem was easier to face than vague fear.

qa.q: What could Sofia do next with what she now knows?
qa.a: Ask her parents how she can help and help Diego understand, since knowing the limits lets the family plan together.

qa.q: How had Diego been seeing the tension?
qa.a: Diego was scared, guessing his parents were getting divorced because nobody had explained anything.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing tension at home, gently asking what changed and learning the father's income has dropped, turning vague worry into a clear problem.
